clinicalPearls: p14 deficiency is a very rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss of the endosomal adaptor protein p14 (LAMTOR2), a component of the Ragulator/LAMTOR complex.
The syndrome combines congenital neutropenia with partial hypopigmentation of skin and hair, short stature and immune dysfunction.
The immune defect spans neutrophils, B lymphocytes and cytotoxic T cells, producing recurrent bronchopulmonary and skin infections.
Partial albinism links it phenotypically to other endosomal and lysosomal biogenesis and trafficking disorders, although its genetic and mechanistic basis is distinct.
Neutrophils show impaired function, B cells generate reduced antibody responses, and cytotoxic lymphocyte killing is impaired.
Recognising the combination of neutropenia, hypopigmentation and growth failure should prompt genetic evaluation.
Management is largely supportive, with infection prophylaxis, growth-factor support for neutropenia and consideration of haematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
reference.pathophysiology: LAMTOR2 encodes the small endosomal adaptor protein p14, a subunit of the Ragulator (LAMTOR) complex anchored to the surface of late endosomes and lysosomes. This complex scaffolds MAPK (MEK/ERK) signalling on endosomes and regulates activation of mTOR complex 1 at the lysosomal membrane, and it is important for endosomal biogenesis and intracellular trafficking. A hypomorphic loss-of-function variant reduces p14 expression, impairing late endosomal function and the associated MAPK and mTOR-dependent processes across multiple cell lineages. The consequences include defective neutrophil, B-cell and cytotoxic T-cell function, disturbed melanosome and pigment biology (accounting for the hypopigmentation) and impaired growth (short stature).
additionalDifferentials: Other combined immunodeficiencies with pigmentary abnormality
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with serial counts to document neutropenia
Immunoglobulin levels and specific antibody responses
Cytotoxic T-cell and natural killer cell cytotoxicity assays
Examination of hair shaft and skin melanocyte pigmentation
redFlags: Congenital or persistent neutropenia with recurrent bacterial infection
Failure to thrive or short stature alongside recurrent infection
Features overlapping haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis where cytotoxic function is impaired
reference.prognosis: Outcome data are limited given the rarity of the disorder; with infection prophylaxis and supportive care many patients do reasonably well, though the multi-lineage immune defect confers ongoing infection risk and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be considered in severe disease.
pitfalls: Attributing hypopigmentation to Chediak-Higashi or Griscelli syndrome without considering p14/LAMTOR2 deficiency.
Overlooking the immunodeficiency when neutropenia dominates the presentation.
Regarding the hypopigmentation as merely cosmetic rather than a clue to an endosomal trafficking disorder.
Failing to assess cytotoxic lymphocyte function and the associated risk of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
references: IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
Clinical immunology reference texts on phagocyte and combined immune defects
management: Prevent infection with prophylactic antimicrobials and treat bronchopulmonary and skin infections promptly and aggressively with appropriate antibiotics and antifungals
Support the neutrophil defect with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor to raise counts during infection or severe neutropenia
Provide immunoglobulin replacement where impaired B-cell antibody responses cause hypogammaglobulinaemia or recurrent infections
Consider haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the potentially curative option in severe multi-lineage immune disease
Monitor serial full blood counts, immunoglobulin levels, specific antibody responses and growth
Offer genetic counselling and family testing for this autosomal recessive LAMTOR2 disorder and manage within a specialist immunology service
